form: 14 Pieces of Spontaneous Discourse in ʔayʔaǰuθəm:

Descriptions of Famous Artworks by Betty Wilson* D. K. E. Reisinger  University of British Columbia Abstract: This paper present s a collection of 14 pieces of spontaneous discourse in ʔayʔaǰuθəm (a.k.a. Comox-Sliammon; ISO 639 -3: coo) — a Coast Salish language spoken along the Strait of Georgia in British Columbia, Canada. In the texts, Betty Wilson, a speaker of the Tla’amin dialect, describes famous pieces of art, ranging from the Renaissance paintings of Sandro Botticelli to the pre-Raphaelite works of John William Waterhouse. Her descriptions were recorded in July 2023 as part of a larger linguistic experiment and show — due to their unscripted and spontaneous nature — a side of the language that is rarely seen in regular elicitation. The texts in this paper are ripe with novel vocabulary, speculative language, and discourse particles, and, thus, form a valuable resource for both linguists and language learners.
Keywords: ʔayʔaǰuθəm (Comox-Sliammon), discourse, texts, discourse particles, determiners

form: In this paper, I present 14 fully glossed pieces of spontaneous discourse in ʔayʔaǰuθəm (a.k.a. Comox-Sliammon; ISO 639 -3: coo) — a Coast Salish language traditionally spoken by four communities in British Columbia, Canada. The texts originated as incidental by-product of a larger linguistic experiment that Marianne Huijsmans and I conducted in the summer of 2023 (see Reisinger & Huijsmans 2024 for details ). While the experiment primarily explored how determiners and demonstratives interact with co-speech gestures in the language, it also included a distractor task in order to make the procedure less monotonous. In this distractor task, we would ask our participants to describe some famous pieces of art that were shown to them on a laptop — ranging from Sandro Botticelli’s enigmatic Renaissance paintings to the works of German romanticists, Canadian impressionists, and English pre-Raphaelites.

* I would like to express my sincere gratitude to Betty Wilson, whose contributions to the documentation of ʔayʔaǰuθəm cannot be overstated. Without her hard work, determination, and linguistic insights, we all would know much less about the language. č̓ɛč̓ɛhaθɛč!  Contact info: daniel.reisinger@ubc.ca

form: While most participants kept their responses predictably short, often saying no more than one or two sentences about the paintings, Betty Wilson — a speaker of the Tla’amin dialect , and a driving force behind the documentation and revitalization of the language — provided much more elaborate and detailed descriptions of the artworks. Her spontaneous and freely delivered responses are a treasure trove of linguistic data, containing hitherto unattested vocabulary, a variety of discourse particles, and a rich banquet of speculative language. For this reason, the texts included in this paper will be of interest to both linguists and language learners alike. This project contributes to a steadily growing corpus of fully glossed textual materials in the language. Particularly over the last few years , a considerable number of ʔayʔaǰuθəm texts have been published (see Watanabe 2019, 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2025; Galligos et al. 2020; J. Davis 2021a, 2021b; Francis et al. 2022; Louie et al. 2025; Dominick et al. [this volume]). These texts — told by a variety of speakers from different generations — include myths, personal narratives, and descriptions of traditional practices and beliefs.

form: This year will also see the publication of two major volumes of narratives in the language. One of them is the first volume of Tales of Tla’amin Elders — a collection of personal narratives by Mary George, which Honoré Watanabe prepared in collaboration with Marion Harry. The other is Stories about Qayχ — an upcoming book of Mink stories as told by Elsie Paul and compiled by the ʔayʔaǰuθəm Lab at UBC.

While most of the texts listed above can be classified as spontaneous and unscripted, it is worth noting that the narrators were usually familiar with the content of their stories. They had already heard the myths, lived the personal experiences, or witnessed the cultural customs they were talking about. The present collection of texts differs in this regard, as Betty Wilson had, to my knowledge, not been familiar with any of the artworks she encountered during the experiment. As a result, her descriptions represent a level of spontane ity hitherto not found in the existing corpus of textual materials.

The remainder of this paper is structured as follows. In Section 2 , I will outline the methodology, from the elicitation of the data to their transcription. Once this has been done, Section 3 will present the fully glossed descriptions of the artworks as provided by Betty Wilson. To highlight the importance of materials like these, Section 4 will offer some first linguistic insights that emerge from these texts. Section 5 concludes.

As mentioned in the introduction, the following texts originated as a by-product of experimental fieldwork. In July 2023, Marianne Huijsmans and I designed an experiment to examine how determiners and demonstratives interact with co-speech gestures in the language. For this purpose, we created a series of 85 test items, each consisting of a video and an image, and asked participants to judge whether the utterances and gestures used in the videos matched the content of the images or not. Due to the large number of test items and the repetitive nature of the procedure, we decided to also include a small distractor task in the experiment. This task aimed to elicit short pieces of natural speech and consisted of 14 filler items that we interspersed in regular intervals between the primary test items. Each of the filler items showed a picture of a famous artwork and was accompanied by an audio prompt in the language: tam k̓ʷʊnɛtʊxʷ ʔə tə namos? (‘What do you see in the picture?’). We presented all these materials to our participants on a laptop, using Microsoft PowerPoint. To keep track of the responses, we recorded each session using either a voice recorder or a smartphone. (For a detailed description of the experiment and its results, see Reisinger and Huijsmans 2024.)

The 14 artworks included in the distractor task cover a broad range of different art styles and subject matters, from the allegorical paintings of the Early Renaissance to the slice-of-life scenes of Impressionism. The following list provides an overview of all the pictures that featured in the experiment, organized in chronological order by their date of creation . Due to their age, a ll the paintings listed here are by now in the public domain.

The following texts all come from an audio recording made by Marianne Huijsmans with Betty Wilson on July 24, 2023 as part of the experiment outlined above. I subsequently transcribed , glossed, and translated the texts to the best of my knowledge. Challenging words, phrases, and sentences were double-checked and clarified during follow-up elicitation with Betty Wilson. The texts in this paper are presented using a four -line notation, as illustrated in (1). In this notation, the first line represents the data in the orthography, the second line provides a phonemic representation including morpheme breaks, the third line shows the corresponding glosses, and the fourth line offers an English translation.1

gloss: the rhetorical filler, like umm or uh, glossed FILLER

form: In my transcriptions, I try to maintain the characteristics of natural speech. Among other things, this includes keeping rhetorical fillers like /naʔa/ (equivalent to umm or uh in English) as well as occasional false starts. Fillers are treated as independent words here, though they can host clitics, which is typically the case when they follow the determiners. False starts are marked by an en-dash (–) directly after the cut-off in the orthography line and glossed as FS in the gloss line, unless it was possible to identify individual morphemes.

1 The abbreviations used in this paper follow the Leipzig Glossing Rules, with the following additions: ACT.INTR ‘active intransitive’, CHAR ‘characteristic’, CONJ ‘conjunction’, CTR ‘control transitive’, DPRT ‘discourse particle’, EPEN ‘epenthetic consonant’, FILLER ‘rhetorical filler’, FS ‘false start’, INT ‘intensifier’, INTJ ‘interjection’, LV ‘linking vowel’, MDL ‘middle’, NTR ‘non-control transitive’ , SB.PASS ‘subordinate passive’, STAT ‘stative’. Suffixes are marked by a hyphen ‘ -’, infixes by angle brackets ‘< >’, reduplicated material by a tilde ‘~’, clitics by an equal sign ‘=’, suprasegmental morphemes by a backslash ‘ \’, and fused morphemes that cannot be segmented by a ‘+’. When metadata are provided, the abbreviation ‘vf’ stands for volunteered forms and ‘vt’ for volunteered translations.

gloss: the oblique marker, often reduced or elided in natural speech

form: Sometimes, in natural speech, speakers also reduce or completely elide certain elements (see, e.g., Watanabe 2003:79; Huijsmans 2023:14). This happens particularly often with the determiners and with the oblique marker /ʔə/. In the orthography line, I try to represent the utterances as faithfully to the recordings as possible and, consequently, do not include any omitted material here. In the second and third lines, however, I try to restore elided material, indicated by brackets [ ] , wherever it is possible. It should be noted, however, that I refrain from restoring elided determiners as it is difficult to predict which form they would take (see Section 4.2 for more details on this).

In this section, I present the descriptions of the 14 artworks as offered by Betty Wilson in the language. The length of the texts varies considerably depending on the subject matter and the complexity of the artwork . While the allegorical paintings by Botticelli, w ith their rich casts of enigmatic characters, elicited longer responses, descriptions dealing with more worldly scenes remained relatively short. The descriptions follow the chronological order presented in Section 2.2 and are always introduced by the respective painting, in case the reader wants to follow what Betty is referring to. The corresponding audio recording can be found on the website of UBCWPL.

Spontaneous pieces of discourse, like the ones above, are a valuable resource for linguistic research, as they show a side of the language that often remains hidden in traditional elicitation. In this section, I will present some preliminary insights emerging from the texts in Section 3, focussing particularly on discourse particles (Section 4.1) and the use of the determiners (Section 4.2).

The texts presented in this paper contain a considerable number of discourse particles, i.e., functional elements that help manage the flow of the discourse in some way or other. In this section, I will briefly discuss the discourse markers ga /ga/, χʷot /x̌ʷət/, and χʷot /x̌ʷit/, which can all be found in the descriptions of the artworks.

18 Just like in the description of Sandro Botticelli’s Primavera (Section 3.1, line 16), the use of the copula hɛɬ /hiɬ/ here is innovative. Again, it seems to take on a referential role in this sentence (roughly: ‘there’).

Generally, t he second -position clitic ga /ga/ most frequently shows up in imperatives and interrogatives. In declaratives, however, it seems to occur considerably less often. J. Davis proposes that this particle has a softening effect, making utterances “friendlier” and “less confrontational” (2012:34). Huijsmans, on the other hand, treats /ga/ as a linking element which indicates that the proposition is “likely given the preceding discourse” (2023:391). This explanation is supported by the fact that speakers will often translate the clitic as ‘so’ or ‘that’s why’, as illustrated in (2).

After all, it is not apparent why the declaratives including /ga/ should be marked as “likely” given the preceding discourse. For instance, why would three women being dancers make it likely that there is a young man, as in (4)? And likewise, why would one character wearing black clothes make it likely that there’s a woman next to them, as in (5)? Expanding the scope of the previous discourse does not resolve these issues either. This suggests that further research will be necessary to explain the contribution of /ga/ in utterances like these.

Another discourse marker that can be found in the descriptions of the paintings is χʷot /x̌ʷət/. Watanabe (2003:530) describes this second-position clitic as a marker that indicates that a clause is hypothetical and further points out that it is often translated as ‘it seems that/like’ or ‘I think/guess that’. Huijsmans (2023:396) refines this analysis and proposes that this clitic indicates that the speaker is not fully committed to the truth of the prejacent.

In the description of t he Max Liebermann painting with the two riders on the beach, we can find one clear instance of this discourse particle, as reproduced in (7). In follow-up elicitation, Betty translated this line with the phrase ‘It looks like’, which is in line with Watanabe’s (2003) and Huijsman’s (2023) observations.
‘It looks like they are talking to each other.’

form: The texts in Section 3 provide also some striking insights concerning the use of the determiners in the language, as I will show in the following paragraphs.

Over the years, many attempts have been made to capture the contribution of the various determiners in the language, for instance by J. Davis (1973:10), Harris (19 77:92), Watanabe (2003:79), and Huijsmans et al. (2018). According to the most recent analyses by Huijsmans et al. (2020) and Reisinger et al. (2021) , the language contains five distinct determiners which vary in terms of evidentiality, gender, and number, as shown in Table 1.
Table 1: The determiner system according to Huijsmans et al. (2020:176).

Current Direct Evidence Previous Direct Evidence Evidence Neutral Gender/Number-Neutral tə šɛ kʷ Feminine SG. ɬə ɬ — In short, Huijsmans et al. (2020) and Reisinger et al. (2021) argue that speakers use the tə /tə/ determiner for referents they have current direct evidence for (i.e., for entities they can see at the time of speaking), while the šɛ /šə/ determiner is used for referents they have previous direct evidence for (i.e., for entities they saw at some point, but that they can no longer see at the time of speaking). When referring to a singular feminine entity (e.g., a woman, a girl, an aunt, a female deer, etc.), the determiners ɬə or ɬ are used instead. They, too, indicate whether the speaker has current or previous direct evidence for the relevant entity, respectively. The determiner kʷ /kʷ/ completes the system. It is neutral in terms of evidence, gender, and number , and consequently often shows up in contexts where the speaker has no direct evidence for the existence of the referent. While the system outlined above makes fairly strong predictions in which situation which determiner would be used, the texts presented in this paper show that, in natural speech, the use of determiners may be much more flexible. Particularly the evidential restrictions, which surface quite clearly in regular elicitation , seem not to apply in many of the texts presented in Section 3 . For instance, in the description of Sandro Botticelli’s Calumny of Apelles, almost the whole inventory of determiners gets used to refer to entities visible in the painting, as shown by the examples in (13) to (15).
